content:
Getting in and out of a bath is hard with painful hips and knees and less strength.

This guide explains wet rooms and other bathroom changes. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why bathrooms are risky

Wet floors, stepping over a bath edge and standing for long periods all increase the risk of falls.

What a wet room can include

  • A level floor with drainage.
  • A shower seat.
  • Grab rails.
  • Lever taps and a thermostatic valve.
  • Non-slip flooring.

Simpler options

  • A bath board or bath lift.
  • A shower over the bath with a seat.
  • A long-handled sponge.

Assessment and funding

Ask your council for an OT assessment. A Disabled Facilities Grant may help with major adaptations; arrangements differ across the UK.

While you wait

  • Wash sitting down.
  • Keep items within reach.
  • Have someone nearby if possible.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I need a full wet room?

Not always; an OT can suggest options.

Will the grant cover it?

It depends on assessment and finances.

Sources and further reading

  • GOV.UK: Disabled Facilities Grants
  • NHS: Home adaptations
  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes
